title: Semiconductor stocks: how to analyze semiconductor companies
description: Semiconductor stocks run on the value chain, the cycle and the gross margin moat — the method with worked examples and sources.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Semiconductor stocks are shares in companies that design or manufacture chips — the circuits sitting in everything from data servers and mobile phones to cars and home appliances. The industry is in a historic expansion: global semiconductor sales reached 627.6 billion dollars in 2024, an increase of 19.1 percent, and 791.7 billion dollars in 2025 (+25.6 percent) according to the industry association SIA — records two years in a row, driven by artificial intelligence. AK1A's analysis universe holds three of the industry's heaviest names: NVIDIA and AMD among the design companies, and contract manufacturer TSMC. Their common denominators — high gross margins, wild order cycles and multiples that demand independent thinking — are this guide's subject. As always here: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are semiconductor stocks — the value chain decides the analysis

The semiconductor industry is not one industry but a chain, and every link has its own economics. **The design companies** — the universe's NVIDIA and AMD — own no factory (the industry jargon says fabless): they draw the circuits and let others manufacture. Their economics are software-like: the universe's raw data (2026-09-15) shows gross margins of 74.7 percent for NVIDIA and 55.7 for AMD, and profit is governed by product cycles, not machine parks. **The contract manufacturers** — foundries — own the factories instead, and a state-of-the-art semiconductor fab costs billions to build before the first chip leaves the line. TSMC, the world's largest, carries a 64.2 percent gross margin and a 56.1 percent operating margin in the universe's data — a combination of capital-heavy commodity industry and almost software-like margins, made possible by a process-technology lead. **The equipment companies** — where the lithography suppliers belong — deliver the machines that make the factories possible, and thereby the industry's own investment cycle: their order books swing with the foundries' appetite for building, and some process steps depend in practice on a single supplier worldwide — a concentration making the entire chain sensitive to individual bottlenecks. Each link is measured differently: design on gross margin and product cycle, foundry on utilization and cost of capital, equipment on order backlog. The course [the Semiconductor Sector](/kurser/se-02-halvledarsektorn) walks through the chain systematically.

## The cycle — the order book and the bullwhip effect

Despite the AI boom, semiconductors are a cyclical industry, and the cycle is amplified by a mechanism logisticians call the bullwhip effect. An example: a computer manufacturer needs 100 chips and orders 110 — ten extra for safety. Next period the customer still needs 100, but 20 chips already sit in inventory: the order becomes 80. Demand fell zero percent — the order decline was still 27 percent. One step up the chain the swing amplifies further, because every link orders with a buffer: that is why chip companies' revenues can fall by half in a downturn where end demand barely moved — precisely the pattern of the last downcycle, when pandemic over-ordering had built inventories that then had to be emptied.

The cycle's early measures live in the balance sheet — and in the order book. Semiconductor companies' reports often show an order backlog: the value of signed but not yet delivered orders. The ratio of new orders to invoiced revenue — the same book-to-bill that industrial companies report — turns months before revenues, and a level below 1.0 means the order backlog is draining while inventories can still look healthy. Inventory days are calculated as inventory divided by cost of goods sold times 365: an inventory of 8 million against an annual cost of goods of 40 million gives 8 ÷ 40 × 365 = 73 days; at 12 million on unchanged cost of goods it becomes 110 days — and rising inventory days on falling orders is the classic receipt that a downcycle has begun. How to measure revenue stability across the cycle is covered in [the revenue stability analysis](/blogg/v12-intaktsstabilitet-analys), and the cycle mechanics in [Cycle risk](/kurser/rk-05-cykelrisk).

## The gross margin — technology's moat

The difference between 74.7 percent (NVIDIA) and 55.7 (AMD) is no coincidence but the industry's central competition question: who gets the customer to pay for its ecosystem? A circuit that is technically best can still be replaced if the entire tool chain — libraries, training, ready-made models — is built around the competitor's platform. Such ecosystems behave like network effects: every new developer who joins makes the platform more valuable for the next, which is one of the strongest moats there is — the mechanism is covered in [Network effects](/kurser/v15-natverkseffekter) and [the network analysis](/blogg/v15-natverkseffekter-analys). The gross margin is where these forces show first: a platform that holds its margin through a price-pressed period has proven its position, and one that is eroded quarter by quarter is losing it. The full craft of the measures is in [Gross margin analysis](/blogg/v07-bruttomarginal-analys).

## The multiple — trailing misleads, forward speaks

The universe's semiconductor trio trades at P/E ratios between 27.8 (TSMC) and 117.5 (AMD) — a span that makes every comparison meaningless without context. As in all industries, the multiple should be compared with the company's own history and with its own group in the chain: a design company against design companies, a foundry against foundries — never design against manufacturing. The reason: the trailing P/E — price divided by the last twelve months' earnings — looks over its shoulder at an industry state about to change. A worked example with universe numbers: NVIDIA's trailing P/E of 28.4 with a consensus forecast of 65.7 percent earnings growth gives a forward multiple of 28.4 ÷ 1.657 ≈ 17 — if the earnings materialize and the price stands still. AMD's 117.5 with a forecast of +104.2 percent gives 117.5 ÷ 2.042 ≈ 58. Still high — but the numbers tell a different story than the trailing figures, and the whole difference lives in the denominator's growth. That is exactly why the PEG ratio exists — multiple divided by growth rate — and exactly as important, why it [has its weaknesses](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026): a forecast is a forecast, and precisely in cyclical industries the consensus is at its most optimistic near the top. Complement with [the P/S ratio](/blogg/ps-tal-nar-ar-det-anvandbart) when earnings are small, and calculate backwards — what growth is priced in? — with [reverse DCF](/kurser/km-028-reverse-dcf).

## How to read the semiconductor company's report

Five details worth extra attention. First, the segments: data center, gaming, cars and industrial parts cycle differently — a company where data center carries everything is a different business than one evenly spread. Second, the gross margin's movement: the moat test from the previous section. Third, inventory in days: rising days on falling orders is the cycle's warning bell. Fourth, geography and export controls: the semiconductor industry sits in the middle of trade politics; tariffs and export bans can move revenues between quarters — read the risk section, not just the income statement. Fifth, the capital outlay for foundries: when is the next fab built, and what does it cost per year? The reading order in [the quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) and [How to read a Swedish annual report](/blogg/sa-laser-du-en-svensk-arsredovisning) applies as the framework.

## The summary

- Sort by value chain first: design (margin + product cycle), foundry (utilization + capital) or equipment (order backlog) — three different economies under one label.
- The cycle is amplified by the bullwhip effect: in the example, orders fell 27 percent on unchanged demand; inventory days (73 → 110) are the early measure.
- The gross margin is the moat test: 74.7 against 55.7 percent in the universe — the ecosystem's network effects show there first.
- The multiple: trailing 27.8–117.5 misleads; the forward calculation (28.4 ÷ 1.657 ≈ 17) speaks — but builds on a forecast.
- Read the report on the industry's terms: segments, gross margin, inventory days, export controls and capital outlay.

Next step in the education track: [the Semiconductor Sector](/kurser/se-02-halvledarsektorn) deepens the chain, [Cycle risk](/kurser/rk-05-cykelrisk) the mechanics, and [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) puts the method in its context.
